target_en: Thus, Tellson’s had become the ultimate example of inconvenience.
"Always rusty!
His fingers are always rusty!" muttered young Jerry. "Where does my father get all that iron rust from?
He certainly doesn't get it around here!"
"You know the Old Bailey courthouse well, no doubt?" said one of the oldest clerks to Jerry the messenger.
"Yes, sir," returned Jerry in a stubborn voice. "I _do_ know the Bailey."
"Just so.
And you know Mr.
Lorry."
"I know Mr.
Lorry, sir, much better than I know the Bailey." He said it the way a reluctant witness answers in court.
"Much better than I, as an honest tradesman, wish to know the Bailey."
"Very well.
Find the door where the witnesses go in, and show the doorkeeper this note for Mr.
Lorry.
He will then let you in."
"Into the courtroom, sir?"
"Into the courtroom."
Mr.
Cruncher’s eyes seemed to get a little closer together, as if asking each other, "What do you think of this?"
"Am I to wait in the court, sir?" he asked, after considering the idea.
"I am going to tell you.
The doorkeeper will pass the note to Mr.
Lorry. You must make some gesture to attract Mr.
Lorry’s attention and show him where you are standing.
Then, your job is simply to stay there until he needs you."
"Is that all, sir?"
"That’s all.
He wants to have a messenger nearby.
This note is just to let him know you have arrived."
As the old clerk slowly folded and addressed the note, Mr.
Cruncher watched him in silence until he began using the blotting paper to dry the ink. Then Jerry remarked:
"I suppose they’ll be trying forgery cases this morning?"
"Treason!"
"That means drawing and quartering," said Jerry. "Barbarous!"
"It is the law," remarked the old clerk, turning his spectacles toward him in surprise. "It is the law."
"I think it’s harsh for the law to ruin a man's body like that.
It’s hard enough to kill him, but it’s very hard to slice him up, sir."
"Not at all," replied the old clerk. "Speak well of the law.
Take care of your own health, my friend, and leave the law to take care of itself.
That is my advice to you."
"It’s the damp weather, sir, that settles in my chest and voice," said Jerry. "You can imagine what a damp way of earning a living mine is."
"Well, well," said the old clerk. "We all have our different ways of making a living.
Some of us have damp ways, and some have dry ways.
Here is the letter.
Off you go."

Jerry took the letter. Under his breath, with far less respect than his polite bow suggested, he muttered, "You are a withered old man yourself." He told his son where he was going as he walked past him. Then he went on his way.
In those days, executions were carried out at Tyburn, so the street outside Newgate Prison had not yet gained the infamous reputation it would have later.

However, the prison itself was a filthy, corrupt place where all kinds of vice and crime were practiced and where terrible diseases bred. These illnesses often came into the courtroom with the prisoners, sometimes spreading directly to the Lord Chief Justice himself and killing him.
More than once, a judge wearing the black execution cap had pronounced his own death sentence along with the prisoner's, dying even before the condemned man did.

Otherwise, the Old Bailey was famous as a deadly departure point. Pale travelers set out from there in carts and carriages, making a violent journey into the next world. They traveled two and a half miles through public streets. Any good citizens who watched had reason to feel ashamed.
Such is the power of custom, showing how important it is to establish good customs in the first place.

The court was also famous for the pillory. It was a punishment where no one could predict how much harm the crowd might do. Then there was the whipping post ,  another beloved tradition. And there was the practice of paying reward money for catching criminals. That system reliably led to terrible crimes committed purely for greed.

Overall, the Old Bailey at that time was a prime example of the lazy saying, "Whatever is, is right." It's a tidy idea. It would be simple and final ,  except that it also means nothing in the past had ever been wrong.
Jerry moved through the dirty crowd with the quiet skill of a man who knew how to go unnoticed. He found the door he was looking for and passed his note through a small slot.
In those days, people paid to watch trials at the Old Bailey just as they paid to watch the patients at Bedlam asylum, except the trials cost much more.
Therefore, all the doors to the Old Bailey were heavily guarded, except for the doors the criminals entered through, which were always left wide open.
After some delay and discussion, the door opened slightly, allowing Mr.
Jerry Cruncher to squeeze himself into the courtroom.
"What's happening?" he whispered to the man standing next to him.
"Nothing yet."
"What case is coming up?"
"The treason case."
"The drawing and quartering one, right?"

"Yes!" the man replied with excitement. "He’ll be dragged on a wooden frame to be half-hanged, then cut down and sliced up while he's still alive. His insides will be pulled out and burned before his eyes, then his head will be chopped off and his body cut into four pieces.
That’s the sentence."
"If he’s found guilty, you mean?" Jerry added, to clarify.
"Oh, they’ll find him guilty," said the other. "Don't you worry about that."
Mr.
Cruncher’s attention was then drawn to the doorkeeper, whom he saw walking toward Mr.
Lorry with the note.
Mr.

Lorry sat at a table among the lawyers in wigs, not far from the prisoner’s defense lawyer, who had a large stack of papers in front of him. Nearly opposite sat another lawyer in a wig, with his hands in his pockets, who seemed entirely focused on staring at the courtroom ceiling.
Whenever Mr. Cruncher looked at him, whether right then or later on, the man seemed to be completely focused on the courtroom ceiling.
It took some effort, but he finally caught Mr. Lorry's eye. Mr.
Lorry had stood up to look for him. He nodded quietly and sat back down.
"What does _he_ have to do with the case?" asked the man Jerry had been talking to.
"I have no idea," said Jerry.
"What do _you_ have to do with it, then, if I may ask?"
"I don't know that either," said Jerry.
The entrance of the Judge and the general movement of the crowd settling into their places stopped their conversation.
Soon, the prisoner's dock became the center of attention.
Two guards who had been standing there stepped out, and the prisoner was brought in and placed at the bar.
Everyone in the courtroom, except the lawyer looking at the ceiling, stared at him.
The breath of the crowd seemed to rush toward him like a wave, a wind, or a fire.

Eager faces leaned around pillars and corners to see him. Spectators in the back rows stood up so they wouldn't miss a single detail. People on the floor put their hands on the shoulders of those in front of them to get a better view. They stood on tiptoe and climbed onto ledges.

Standing out among them was Jerry. He looked like a piece of the spiked wall of Newgate Prison. He breathed out the smell of the beer he had drunk on the way. That smell joined the thick, damp air of the crowded room ,  the air that was slowly misting up the large windows behind the prisoner.
The target of all this attention was a young man of about twenty-five, tall, well-built, with sunburnt skin and dark eyes.
He looked like a young gentleman.
He was dressed plainly in black or dark gray, and his long, dark hair was tied back with a ribbon, more to keep it out of the way than for style.
Just as strong emotions show through any clothing, the paleness caused by his dangerous situation showed through his sunburned cheeks, proving that his inner feelings were stronger than the sun.
Otherwise, he was quite calm, bowed to the Judge, and stood quietly.
The interest with which the crowd stared and breathed on this man was not a noble human feeling.
If he had been facing a less terrible sentence, or if there had been any chance he would be spared its brutal details, he would have been far less fascinating to them.
The body that was doomed to be so horribly mutilated was the main attraction; the human being about to be butchered was the source of the excitement.
Whatever excuses the spectators made for their interest, at its root, it was a savage, monstrous curiosity.
"Silence in court!" was called.

Charles Darnay had pleaded not guilty the day before to a long, repetitive indictment charging him with being a traitor to our king. He was accused of having assisted Louis, the King of France, in his wars against England on several occasions. The charges claimed he did this by traveling back and forth between England and France, revealing to the French king what military forces England was preparing to send to Canada and North America.

Jerry's hair seemed to stand up even more as the complicated legal terms were read. He listened with satisfaction. He figured out that this Charles Darnay was indeed the man on trial. The jury was being sworn in.
The Attorney General was preparing to speak.
